# 1.2 Example 1

## Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

The first thing we want to do when faced with a passage is ask
ourselves, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us
that something is true?"**

So, let's start by asking that question of this piece of text:

> "Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product. Therefore,
> there's no need to research items before making a major purchase."

It seems to me that this passage is trying to prove that there's no need
to research items before making a major purchase. It's trying to
convince us of this by citing another claim as evidence, so this passage
does contain an argument.

Of course, this passage might not contain a very *good* argument because
it might not be doing a very *good job* of proving that there's no need
to research items before making a major purchase, but it is *trying* to
prove this, and that's what matters.

### What Inference Indicator Expressions Are and Why They Matter

The most basic way to recognize an argument is to do what we just did:
ask ourselves, "Is this passage trying to convince us that something is
true?" If so, it's an argument. If not, it isn't.

The bad news is that this question can be difficult to answer. The good
news is that there is a short cut that we can use sometimes.

Remember, all arguments try to prove that a claim is true by citing
other claims as evidence. The connection between the evidence and the
claim being proven true is an *inference*. Thus, *all arguments have
inferences*. In fact, the reverse is true, too. Any passage that
contains an inference is an argument, so **once we see that a passage
contains an inference, we can be certain that it contains an argument as
well**.

How, then, can we spot those crucial inferences? That's a great
question. After all, an inference is the connection that binds one claim
to another, just like a bridge is the connection between two boulders.
This means that the inference *itself* isn't a claim that can be written
down as a sentence and pointed to in the argument, and sometimes it
won't correspond to *anything* that we can point to in the passage. (We
can think of an inference as the force between two magnets instead of a
bridge between two boulders. In a simple argument, for example, the
premise is the first magnet, the ultimate conclusion is the second
magnet, and the inference is the force that holds the two together. Just
like we can see the magnets but can only gesture in the general
direction of the magnetic force, we can put our fingers on an argument's
premise and ultimate conclusion but can only indicate where that
invisible inference is.)

*Occasionally*, however, we'll get lucky, and inferences will be
expressed using certain terms -- words we *can* point a finger at. This
means that **we can *sometimes* recognize an argument by spotting these
special "inference indicator" expressions**. And don't worry. Once you
get used to seeing inferences with the help of inference indicator
expressions, it will be easier to see them when inference indicator
expressions aren't there because you'll be used to detecting the
underlying relationship between claims.

In the argument that we're considering, for example, the inference
indicator expression is "therefore."

> "Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, there's no need to research items before making a major
> purchase."

This "therefore" shows us that there's an inference between "every
advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely accurate and
comprehensive information about the product," and "there's no need to
research items before making a major purchase." It shows us, in other
words, that one of these claims (which we call the "reason") is being
given as a reason to believe the other claim (which we call the
"conclusion").

***It's impossible to overestimate the importance of inference indicator
expressions!*** Many of the most common problems that people run into
later stem *directly* from their unfamiliarity with the inference
indicator expression, so it's essential to learn how to recognize and
use them.

Now that we've seen that our passage contains an argument, let's analyze
it.

## Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

### The Importance of Analysis

Analyzing an argument enables us to fully understand it, and we'll want
to understand the argument *before* we start evaluating it. There will
be many opportunities to evaluate the argument later, but if we don't
take the time to understand the argument first, there's the danger that
our assessment of the argument, our agreement or disagreement with it,
will be based upon a misinterpretation of the argument.

Patiently understanding a position before passing judgment upon it is
also the *kind* thing to do. We shudder to think how many fights and
hurt feelings could have been avoided if people had only *stopped to
understand what the other person was saying before jumping in to
disagree.*

*"**Listen first and listen well**"* is a motto that will serve us
admirably in every context. *"**Analyze before evaluating**,"* is an
instance of this motto, and the first rule of good reasoning.

### Identifying Claims and Connections, and Mapping the Argument

Analyzing an argument consists of correctly identifying the **claims**
that compose the argument and accurately tracking the **connections**
between those claims.

The first claim we want to identify, if possible, is the ultimate
conclusion so the first question we should ask ourselves when analyzing
an argument is, **"What is the ultimate conclusion, the main claim that
this argument is trying to get us to believe?"**

We'll number the important claims in order to make it easy to refer to
them later, and because the ultimate conclusion is the first claim that
we try to identify, we'll always give it number "1."

As you might remember, we already identified the ultimate conclusion of
this argument - it's "There's no need to research items before making a
major purchase" -- so we can indicate that in the text.

> "Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

And now we can appreciate an additional function of that inference
indicator word "therefore."

We've already seen that "therefore" shows us that there's an inference
between "every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
accurate and comprehensive information about the product," and "there's
no need to research items before making a major purchase."

But it does *more* than that, doesn't it? In addition to telling us
*that* one claim is supposed to follow from another, the "therefore"
tells us *which* claim is supposed to follow from another: specifically,
it tells us that "there's no need to research items before making a
major purchase" is the *conclusion* that's supposed to follow from
"every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
accurate and comprehensive information about the product."

For this reason, we'll call inference indicator expressions like
"therefore" "conclusion indicator expressions." **We can think about
conclusion indicator expressions like signs that say, "Here comes a
conclusion!"**

There are a *lot* of inference indicator expressions that work like
"therefore" and introduce conclusions. Here is a list of some of the
most common.

Conclusion Indicator Expressions:

-   \[reason\]. Therefore \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Thus \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Consequently \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Hence \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\], so \[conclusion\] / \[reason\], and so \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] implies \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] which means that \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] which goes to show that \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. As a result, \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. That's why \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. It follows that \[conclusion\].

Once we've identified the ultimate conclusion, we'll want to return to
the beginning of the passage and ask ourselves, **"What else is being
claimed?"** And **"Is this claim part of the argument?"**

"Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
accurate and comprehensive information about the product" is another
claim in the passage, and it's part of the argument, too, because it's
being given as evidence for the ultimate conclusion. Let's give this new
claim number "2," so that we can refer to it later.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

Now we can ask our next question, **"How are these claims connected to
each other?"**

As will often be the case, **the inference indicator expression helps us
out**. (These expressions are *very important*.) The "therefore," a
conclusion indicator, tells us that "(1) There's no need to research
items before making a major purchase," is a conclusion that follows from
"(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
accurate and comprehensive information about the product." In other
words, "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer
completely accurate and comprehensive information about the product,"
supports "(1) There's no need to research items before making a major
purchase." We'll call this "the support relationship" and define it as
follows:

> **A reason supports a conclusion when the reason is being given as a
> reason to believe that the conclusion is true.**

We can graphically represent the relationship of support like this, with
the conclusion on the top and the reason on the bottom. The inference is
the line connecting the reason to the claim that it's supporting.

![The support relationship: a conclusion on top, supported by a reason on the bottom.](/images/ch01/Reason_Conclusion.png){#fig-1-2-general width=124px fig-alt="Argument map: a conclusion at the top, supported by a reason through an inference. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-general"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Reason_Conclusion_list.md >}}
:::

**The graphical representation of an argument is called an "argument
map."** As we noted when looking at our Sunshine Soda example, argument
maps show us how all of the claims in an argument are connected to each
other and this makes complex arguments *much* easier to understand.
That's why we'll always analyze arguments by mapping them.

The map of the argument we're considering would look like this:

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1.png){#fig-1-2-ad-1 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_list.md >}}
:::

(We will label the inference lines with capital letters to make them
easier to discuss when we see more structurally complex arguments
later.)

If we don't want to re-write the claims, we can just refer to them by
number—which, after all, is why we numbered them in the first place.
We can also write "A" instead of "Inference A" because we know that the
green line is an inference. This would give us the following map:

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![The advertisement argument mapped with claim numbers only.](/images/ch01/1_A_2.png){#fig-1-2-ad-numbers width=68px fig-alt="Argument map: claim 1 at the top, supported by claim 2 through inference A. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-numbers"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/1_A_2_list.md >}}
:::

We will usually put entire claims in the boxes and not just the numbers
because this reduces the need to refer to the passage. If you are
mapping by hand, however, it's often easier to number claims in the
passage and then simply use the numbers in your map.

All of the arguments in this chapter will have the simplest possible
argument structure: one premise on the bottom, an ultimate conclusion at
the top, and an inference connecting them, so they'll all be mapped the
same way. Arguments will get more complicated before long, but for now,
we'll take advantage of this structural simplicity to focus on the
fundamentals of argument analysis and evaluation.

And it's worth noting that I said the arguments in this chapter have the
simplest possible *structure*. When I say that these arguments are
simple, I mean that their *maps* are simple, not that their content is
simple or that the process of analyzing or evaluating them is simple, so
if you find some of these arguments tricky, fear not! Hydrogen,
consisting of one proton and one electron, is the element with the
simplest structure, but the process of discovering that structure was
not easy!

Now that we have our argument analyzed, let's evaluate it.

## Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

Because an argument is a unit of reasoning that attempts to establish that
a claim is true by citing other claims as evidence, **an argument is
good if it *does* establish that the ultimate conclusion is probably
true. If it *doesn't* establish that the conclusion is probably true, on
the other hand, then the argument is bad.** Furthermore, the features of
an argument that help or prevent an argument from establishing the truth
of its conclusion are the only things that we want to spend time on.
Other features of an argument (like how well it's written, for example)
might be nice to notice, but they don't affect whether or not the
argument is good or bad *as an argument*.

So, let's look at our example argument again.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1.png){#fig-1-2-ad-2 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_list.md >}}
:::

Is this argument good? Does it successfully establish that the
conclusion is true?

I don't think so. After all, do you now believe... *honestly believe*...
that there's no need to research items before making a major purchase?
No, probably not. (If you decided that the argument is good, you might
have been thinking that you could understand *someone else* believing
the ultimate conclusion on the basis of that premise, or something like
that. But right now, don't think that hard. Just ask yourself, "Does
this argument convince *me* that the ultimate conclusion is true? Do I,
after reading this, *really believe* that there's no need to research
items before making a major purchase?" And I bet you don't.)

The fact that this argument hasn't given us reason to believe its
ultimate conclusion means that the argument is bad. But *why* is it bad?
What has gone wrong?

It might be tempting to think that this argument is bad because the
ultimate conclusion is false. In fact, the ultimate conclusion here *is*
false but, strangely enough, **we never evaluate the ultimate conclusion
of an argument when we evaluate the argument. This is because the
central issue is whether or not the argument gives us good reason to
believe the ultimate conclusion, not whether or not the ultimate
conclusion is actually true.** What's the difference? Well, the
conclusion can be true even if the argument doesn't give us good reason
to think that it is. We'll talk more about this later.

So, if the problem with this argument isn't that the ultimate conclusion
is false, what is the problem? The problem is that the *premise* is
false. Advertisements *aren't* designed to give the consumer completely
accurate and comprehensive information about the product; they're
designed to sell the product, and sometimes don't give the consumer any
information about the product *at all*. (Think about the last commercial
you saw that paired the product with images of popularity, for example.
The advertiser's hope is that you'll identify the product with
popularity and so want to buy it -- not that you'll learn a wealth of
information about the product.)

We can note in the map that the premise is bad.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-2-ad-eval-1 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-eval-1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Since the premises are given as reason for us to believe the ultimate
conclusion, and since false premises can't give us reason to believe
anything (just like fabricated evidence can't *really* prove that the
defendant in a trial is guilty or innocent), a false premise makes the
argument bad.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-2-ad-eval-2 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-eval-2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it has a false premise.

### Evaluating Premises

We've seen that the first thing we should do when looking at a premise
is ask ourselves, **"Is this premise true?"**

We can call an objection to an argument that asserts that a premise is
false a "'not so' objection" because it looks at a premise and says, in
effect, "That's not so."

**A good argument needs true premises**. This is an important rule of
evaluating arguments.

Some people are troubled by this rule. They point out that sometimes we
don't *know* whether a premise is true or false, that sometimes premises
we *think* are true are *actually* false, and that sometimes premises we
think are *false* are actually *true*. These people worry that such
ignorance and error make it virtually impossible to tell whether or not
a premise is true, and if we can't tell whether or not a premise is true
then we can't evaluate an argument on the basis of the truth of its
premises.

This is a very good point, but things aren't as bleak as they seem as
long as we're willing to admit when we don't know something and are
happy to acknowledge when we've been wrong. In fact, **the ability to
admit that we don't know something and the willingness to accept our
mistakes and change our minds are very important *everywhere***. If you
don't know something, say, "I don't know," and if you've been mistaken
say, "I've been mistaken." Not knowing something isn't so bad; nobody
knows everything. Being wrong isn't so bad; everyone is wrong sometimes.
But pretending that we know things that we don't know and insisting that
we're right when we know we're wrong will bring us *no end* of grief.

If we don't know whether a premise is true or false, we might not be
able to decide if the argument is good or bad. If we're mistaken in our
assessment of the premise, we may be mistaken in our evaluation of the
argument. That's okay. Ignorance and error are part of the human
condition. We just need to be honest with ourselves and do the best with
what we think we know.

** **

### Communicating Our Evaluation

Strange as it might seem, it's *one* thing to be able to evaluate an
argument and quite *another thing* to be able to articulate our
evaluation to other people. And perhaps, upon reflection, that isn't too
surprising. Surely, we've all been in the position of having a pretty
good idea of what we want to say and still being unsure about how to say
it.

As we go along, then, it will be good to learn a few specific things
that we can say to communicate our evaluation of an argument. Obviously,
there are *many ways* that we can articulate our objections, so don't
feel like you need to use exactly the same words that I'll give you
here. Nevertheless, it *is* often very useful to memorize specific
wording, at least at first, because it makes things easier. When you're
learning a new language, for example, you don't need to learn a dozen
different ways to ask for directions to the bathroom. Mastering one
solid, dependable, way is just fine. The same principle applies here.

**If an argument has a false premise, like the argument we've just seen,
we can say, "This argument assumes \[state the premise\], and that's
false because \[state why you think the premise is false\]."**

In the case of this argument, for example, we can say, "This argument
assumes that every advertisement is designed to give the consumer
completely accurate and comprehensive information about the product, and
that's not true because advertisements are designed to sell the product,
and sometimes they don't give the consumer any information about the
product at all."

Note that we didn't mention the author of the argument. **Our task is to
evaluate the *reasoning,* not criticize the reasoner and so we shouldn't
personally attack the individual advancing the argument**. Most
obviously, this principle rules out labeling and name-calling. Less
obviously, it rules out giving the impression that the author of the
argument was stupid, lazy, corrupt, or otherwise negligent for failing
to see the problems in their reasoning. And because of this, we should
portray our objections as non-obvious whenever possible. We can, after
all, safely assume that the author of the argument didn't anticipate our
objections, and so it can be insulting to present those objections as
something that any thinking person should have considered.

This principle can be difficult to apply when the topic of the argument
is deeply contentious and the author of the argument is defending a
viewpoint with which we strongly disagree, but it's in *just such
situations* that this principle is *most important* because if we engage
the author and not the argument, the disagreement will only become more
heated and counterproductive. Nobody will be trying to deepen
understanding or seek the truth because everybody will be too busy
defending themselves, lashing out at others, and scoring cheap debating
points. We've all seen this happen. Sometimes, of course, the author of
the argument won't be extending you the same courtesy that you are
extending to them, but nobody goes anywhere unless somebody takes the
high road. Sometimes that somebody will have to be you, and sometimes
you will walk the high road alone. That's frustrating and it's
maddening, but it's still the best path forward because the low road is
*very* muddy.

But what if the person advancing the argument doesn't genuinely want to
engage in a meaningful conversation about ideas? What if that person is
simply a bully, advancing an argument to *appear* rational while trying
to force their personal or political beliefs on others? It would be
naïve to pretend that never happens and it's hard to know how to respond
when it does. Generally speaking, however, **there are two ways to
effect change in the world: reasoning (participating in a cooperative
dialog that's aimed at the pursuit of truth) or wrestling (fighting it
out with other people in order to dominate them and impose one's own
will)**. If it becomes clear that someone is *actually* wrestling when
it *looks* like they're reasoning, we can still engage their reasoning
in the hopes of nudging the dynamics of the larger conversation in a
more fruitful direction. If the situation is dire, of course, and if
lives are at stake, we can wrestle back. But **it's prudent to wrestle
only as a last resort, because if we wrestle more than we reason,
decisions will be made by the strongest, not by the wisest**.

### Thoughts about the Ultimate Conclusion

Before we leave this argument, let's pause to remind ourselves that when
we evaluated this argument, we did *not* evaluate the ultimate
conclusion. In fact, **we will never evaluate the ultimate conclusion of
an argument when we evaluate the argument itself**. This is because the
central issue is whether or not the argument has given us good reason to
believe the ultimate conclusion, and not whether or not the ultimate
conclusion is actually true. (Can you see the difference? An argument
can give us a bad reason to believe something that just happens to be
true. We'll be talking about this later.)

Nonetheless, **we can expect our evaluation of an argument to have some
bearing upon our acceptance or rejection of the conclusion**. As a first
step in working toward an understanding of what this relationship might
be, let's take a look at the argument we just evaluated. We saw that
this argument is bad. And, furthermore, we know that the ultimate
conclusion is false.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-2-ad-eval-3 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-eval-3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it has a false premise.\
Note 2: This argument happens to have a false conclusion.

Thus, we've seen that **a bad argument can have a false ultimate
conclusion**. This might not be much of a discovery, but it is something
and it takes us part of the way (specifically, one fourth of the way)
toward a complete understanding of the relationship between an argument
and its ultimate conclusion.

For now, let's summarize what we've learned in this example.

## Summary of Example 1

We've finished working through our first example!

> "Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product. Therefore,
> there's no need to research items before making a major purchase."

### Step 1 – Recognizing an Argument

We asked, **"What is this passage doing? Is it trying to convince us
that something is true?"**

If a passage is trying to convince us of something, it contains an
argument. We decided that this passage does contain an argument: it's
trying to convince us that there's no need to research items before
making a major purchase.

Inference indicator expressions, like "therefore," can help us to
recognize arguments, too, because all arguments have inferences.

> "Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, there's no need to research items before making a major
> purchase."

### Step 2 – Analyzing the Argument

To analyze this argument, the first question we asked was, **"What is
the ultimate conclusion, or the main claim that this argument is trying
to get us to believe?"**

We decided that the ultimate conclusion was "there's no need to research
items before making a major purchase."

The inference indicator expression "therefore" can help us here as well
because in addition to telling us that there's an inference in the
passage, "therefore" shows us how the inference works by acting like a
sign that says, "Here comes a conclusion!" **"Therefore" is a conclusion
indicator expression.**

We will always give the ultimate conclusion number 1.

> "Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

There are a lot of conclusion expressions like "therefore." Here's a
list of some of them:

Conclusion Indicator Expressions:

-   \[reason\]. Therefore \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Thus \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Consequently \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. Hence \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\], so \[conclusion\] / \[reason\], and so \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] implies \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] which means that \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\] which goes to show that \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. As a result, \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. That's why \[conclusion\].

-   \[reason\]. It follows that \[conclusion\].

We then returned to the beginning of the passage and asked, **"What else
is being claimed?"** And **"Is this claim part of the argument?"** This
allowed us to identify and number the other claim, "Every advertisement
is designed to give the consumer completely accurate and comprehensive
information about the product."

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

Finally, we asked, **"How are these claims connected to each other?"**

Once again, the conclusion indicator helped us to see that claim 2 was
supporting claim 1.

This gave us the following map of the argument, with the conclusion (1)
on the top, the reason (2) on the bottom, and the inference represented
as a green line between the conclusion and the reason. (We labeled the
inference for easy reference.):

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1.png){#fig-1-2-ad-3 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_list.md >}}
:::

### Step 3 – Evaluating the Argument

An argument is good if and only if it establishes that its ultimate
conclusion is probably true. In order to establish that the ultimate
conclusion is probably true, an argument needs true premises.
Accordingly, a good question to ask when we evaluate an argument is
**"Is this premise true?"**

The premise in this argument isn't true, which makes the argument bad as
a whole.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-2-ad-eval-4 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-eval-4"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it has a false premise.

Objections to the effect that a premise is false are called 'not so'
objections.

When we communicate a "not so" objection we can say, "This argument
assumes \[state the premise\], and that's false because \[state why you
think the premise is false\]."

We should always remember that our task is to evaluate the reasoning and
not criticize the reasoner. This means that we shouldn't personally
attack the author of the argument. It's also a good idea to avoid giving
the impression that the person advancing the argument was stupid, lazy,
corrupt, or negligent for failing to see the problems in their
reasoning.

#### Thoughts about the Ultimate Conclusion

We noted that although we won't ever evaluate the conclusion as part of
our evaluation of the argument, we *will* want to understand the
relationship between arguments and the conclusions they support. Because
the conclusion of this argument is almost certainly false, it shows us
that a bad argument can have a false conclusion.

> "(2) Every advertisement is designed to give the consumer completely
> accurate and comprehensive information about the product.
> **Therefore**, (1) there's no need to research items before making a
> major purchase."

![Map of the advertisement argument, with the premise evaluated as false.](/images/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval.png){#fig-1-2-ad-eval-5 width=351px fig-alt="Argument map concluding: 1) There’s no need to research items before making a major purchase. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-1-2-ad-eval-5"}
{{< include /outlines/ch01/Advertisement1_P_Eval_list.md >}}
:::

Note 1: This argument is bad because it has a false premise.\
Note 2: This argument happens to have a false conclusion.
